# Pre-flight checklist

Run this checklist against the document before delivering it. If an item fails, revise. If it cannot be fixed without losing meaning, note the exception and why.

## Principle 1 — Relevant

- [ ] The intended readers are named or clearly implied.
- [ ] The primary audience is identifiable if multiple audiences exist.
- [ ] The document opens with what readers need to know or do, not with background.
- [ ] Every section serves a reader need, not an author instinct.
- [ ] Nothing readers do not need is included.
- [ ] Nothing readers do need has been left out.
- [ ] Content is accurate. Nothing misleads.

## Principle 2 — Findable

- [ ] The headline states what the document is and what it asks for.
- [ ] The most important message appears within the first screen or first page.
- [ ] If there are several audiences, each has a section they can jump to.
- [ ] Warnings appear before the instructions they warn about.
- [ ] Processes appear in the order they happen.
- [ ] Information most readers need appears before information only some readers need.
- [ ] Headings describe what follows — a reader can grasp the argument by reading only headings.
- [ ] Headings use a clear hierarchy (H1, H2, H3) that matches the content structure.
- [ ] Important elements are visually prominent (bold, tables, callouts).
- [ ] Related elements are grouped together.
- [ ] Elements with the same function look the same.
- [ ] Supplementary detail is labelled and placed after the main content.

## Principle 3 — Understandable

- [ ] Familiar, everyday words are used where possible.
- [ ] Technical terms are defined on first use or in a glossary.
- [ ] Every abbreviation is spelled out on first use.
- [ ] Every concept uses one term consistently. No synonyms.
- [ ] Sentences use active voice by default.
- [ ] Each sentence contains one idea.
- [ ] Sentences state things positively ("arrive by 9" not "do not arrive after 9").
- [ ] Lists use parallel construction (each item starts the same way, uses the same tense).
- [ ] Average sentence length is 15–20 words.
- [ ] Filler and hedges have been cut.
- [ ] Each paragraph has one main idea, stated at the beginning.
- [ ] Paragraphs are short (3–5 sentences).
- [ ] Lists are used for parallel items instead of long prose.
- [ ] Images, diagrams, or tables are used where they help.
- [ ] Every image is labelled and has a text alternative.
- [ ] The tone is respectful, direct, and non-condescending.
- [ ] "You" is used to address the reader.
- [ ] The document reads as a single coherent piece.
- [ ] Cross-references are used instead of repeating content.

## Principle 4 — Usable

- [ ] Sections addressed to teams or roles, not to named individuals (unless the POC is confirmed and stable).
- [ ] The document has been reviewed at least once against this checklist.
- [ ] The document tells the reader how to respond or act.
- [ ] The document tells the reader where to go for more.

## Red flags

Any of these suggest a rewrite:

- The document opens with "This document…" and then a description.
- The reader has to reach page 2 to find the ask.
- Different sections use different names for the same thing.
- Any sentence is more than 30 words.
- Any paragraph is more than 6 sentences.
- Any acronym is unexplained.
- Passive voice appears without a reason.
- Contractions appear in a document for non-native readers.
- The word "TL;DR" appears.
- The document does not tell the reader what to do next.
- Marketing verbs appear ("leverage", "synergise", "empower", "unlock", "drive").
- Weasel words hide uncertainty ("we believe", "it seems", "arguably", "potentially").
- Vague timing ("soon", "recently", "in the coming weeks") appears instead of dates.
- Modal verbs are mixed carelessly — "must", "should", "could", "would" used as if interchangeable.
- Ownership is attributed to more than one team with no primary named.
- A constraint is stated without its reason.
- A review request is vague ("please review and provide feedback").
- Success criteria are missing or vague ("we’ll iterate").
- The document has no date, no version, and no author in the header.
- A cross-reference has no link ("as discussed in the Q2 review").
- Rhetorical questions appear as headings.
- Nested lists go more than two levels deep.
